title: Genie Sim Benchmark: Real-to-Sim Fidelity and Evaluation
trick: Fine-tune one pi0.5 policy per task on real data, score it with equal trials in the real cell and its simulated copy across 22 robot-task pairs, and correlate the two score columns.
framing_stripped: Called 'Real-to-Sim Fidelity and Evaluation' with 'three complementary evidence layers' (execution, interaction, task); it is (a) a 22-row table of real and simulated task Scores for real-data-fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ policies, each row a different (robot, task, policy) triple, summarised by one Pearson $r = 0.9686$ that the paper itself calls 'descriptive' and reports without intervals (sec. II-E, Table B1); (b) a standard three-stage constrained rigid-body identification of two 7-joint arms from motor current, scored on one 32.65 s teleoperation recording (sec. IV-A, Table C3); and (c) five single-episode object replays in which a MuJoCo-fitted contact model is frozen and re-run in MuJoCo-Warp and PhysX, where one of them (the sponge) goes from 25.50 mm to 524.61 mm error and is rescued by hand-set PhysX finger stiffness and damping (sec. IV-B2, App. D.3). The task-level correlation and the physics studies are separate experiments on separate units; the paper states that the physics studies 'do not establish an asset-linked benchmark benefit' (sec. IV-A) and 'do not establish a causal reduction in benchmark task-score discrepancy' (sec. IV-B3).
method_equations: Task score (sec. II-C): within one fixed layout with $S$ scored stages and $N$ recorded episodes, $$\mathrm{Score} = \frac{1}{NS} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{s=1}^{S} c_{is},$$ where $c_{is}$ is the credit recorded for stage $s$ of episode $i$ (its range is not stated in the text; the platform 'records completed substeps and failure stages', sec. II-A); the evaluator 'rounds instruction-level stage means, weights them by recorded episode counts and rounds the result to four decimals'. A separate binary E2E field is 1 when the last scored entry is 1; Score, E2E and binary task success are 'distinct'. Real Scores are assigned manually by test personnel, simulated Scores automatically under 'the aligned evaluation criteria' (sec. II-C). Agreement (sec. II-E): for pair $i \in \{1, \ldots, 22\}$, $\Delta_i = \mathrm{Sim}_i - \mathrm{Real}_i$; $\mathrm{MAE} = \frac{1}{22}\sum_i |\Delta_i| = 0.0405$, $\mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{22}\sum_i \Delta_i^2} = 0.0520$, mean signed gap $\frac{1}{22}\sum_i \Delta_i = -0.0068$, all pairs equal weight; $$r = \frac{\sum_i (\mathrm{Real}_i - \bar{R})(\mathrm{Sim}_i - \bar{S})}{\sqrt{\sum_i (\mathrm{Real}_i - \bar{R})^2 \, \sum_i (\mathrm{Sim}_i - \bar{S})^2}} = 0.9686,$$ with $\bar{R}$, $\bar{S}$ the means of the 22 real and simulated Scores (Table B1; recomputed from the two-decimal table: 0.9689). Units: 22 (configuration, task) pairs: G1 Omnipicker 8, G2 Swiftpicker 6, G2 Wuji 1, Arx X5 7, over 16 task names (Table A1); rollouts per pair 30, 50 or 100 (Table B1), 'real and simulation use equal counts'; summing Table B1 gives 1,340 episodes per world (operator sum). Policy per pair: for the G2 and Arx pairs 'the $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on real-robot data collected for the corresponding task', one task-specific model 'evaluated by inference in both the real and simulated environments' (sec. II-D); for the 8 G1 pairs the Scores 'are taken from the experiments reported in Genie Sim 3.0' and the policy is unknown (not in text). Identification comparison (Table B2): the 14 G2/Arx pairs re-scored in simulation before and after system identification against the same real reference: $r$ 0.9518 to 0.9669, MAE 0.0554 to 0.0443, RMSE 0.0653 to 0.0551; 8 gaps shrink, 1 grows (Arx Recognize Size, $-0.08$ to $-0.11$), 5 unchanged. Real Scores span 0.24 to 1.00 (operator: standard deviation 0.207), so $r \approx \sqrt{1 - \mathrm{var}(\Delta)/\mathrm{var}(\mathrm{Sim})} = 0.964$ follows from the gap-to-spread ratio alone. Robot identification (sec. IV-A1, eq. 1): per arm, at time sample $k$, $$\boldsymbol{\tau}_{I,k} = \mathbf{Y}_k \boldsymbol{\pi} + \mathrm{diag}(\ddot{\mathbf{q}}_k)\, \mathbf{J}_a + \boldsymbol{\tau}_f(\dot{\mathbf{q}}_k) + \mathbf{b}_\tau + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_k,$$ where $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{I,k} \in \mathbb{R}^7$ is motor current converted to joint-side torque, component $\tau_{I,j,k} = p_j K_{t,j} n_j i_{j,k}$ ($i_{j,k}$ current in A, $K_{t,j}$ fixed torque constant in N m/A, $n_j$ reduction ratio, $p_j \in \{-1, 1\}$ sign); $\mathbf{Y}_k = \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{q}_k, \dot{\mathbf{q}}_k, \ddot{\mathbf{q}}_k) \in \mathbb{R}^{7 \times 70}$ the Pinocchio rigid-body regressor; $\boldsymbol{\pi} \in \mathbb{R}^{70}$ the ten standard inertial parameters of each of seven links (mass $m_i$, first moments $\mathbf{h}_i = m_i \mathbf{c}_i$, six inertia-tensor entries; eq. 2); $\mathbf{J}_a \in \mathbb{R}^7$ armature in kg m$^2$; $\mathbf{b}_\tau \in \mathbb{R}^7$ a constant current-to-torque offset; $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_k$ the residual; friction $\tau_{f,j,k} = f_{c,j} \tanh(\dot{q}_{j,k}/C_0) + f_{v,j} \dot{q}_{j,k}$ with Coulomb $f_{c,j} \geq 0$ (N m), viscous $f_{v,j} \geq 0$ (N m s/rad), $C_0 = 0.001$ rad/s. Unknowns: $70 + 7 + 14 + 7 = 98$ per arm; constraints: each link pseudo-inertia positive semidefinite, mass within 50-150% of URDF/CAD, nonnegative armature and friction. Three stages (sec. IV-A2): (1) friction from 20 constant-speed plateaus per joint (0.0087-3.0 rad/s), paired-direction medians $v_\ell = [\mathrm{med}(\dot{q}_+) - \mathrm{med}(\dot{q}_-)]/2$, $z_\ell = [\mathrm{med}(\tau_{I,+}) - \mathrm{med}(\tau_{I,-})]/2$, residual $r_\ell = f_{c,j}\tanh(v_\ell/C_0) + f_{v,j} v_\ell - z_\ell$ (eq. 3), nonnegative Huber IRLS; (2) armature from single-joint sines at 0.5-1.5 Hz, $$\min \; \frac{1}{N_j}\sum_k \rho_1(e_{j,k}) + \lambda_\pi \|\mathbf{D}_\pi(\boldsymbol{\pi} - \boldsymbol{\pi}^{\mathrm{URDF}})\|_2^2 + \lambda_f \|\mathbf{D}_f(\mathbf{f}_j - \mathbf{f}_j^{(1)})\|_2^2$$ (eq. 4) with $e_{j,k}$ predicted minus measured torque, $\rho_1$ the Huber loss with threshold $\delta = 1$ N m, $\lambda_\pi = 1.0$, $\lambda_f = 0.1$, $\mathbf{D}_\pi, \mathbf{D}_f$ diagonal inverse-prior scalings, $\mathbf{f}_j = [f_{c,j}, f_{v,j}]^T$ and $\mathbf{f}_j^{(1)}$ its stage-1 estimate; (3) coupled seven-joint five-harmonic Fourier trajectory (20 s period, cycles 2-4 fitted, cycle 5 reserved), $\min_{\boldsymbol{\pi}, \mathbf{b}_\tau} \frac{1}{N_\tau}\sum_r \rho_1(u_r) + 0.5\|\mathbf{D}_\pi(\boldsymbol{\pi} - \boldsymbol{\pi}^{(2)})\|_2^2$ (eq. 5) with armature and friction frozen at stage-2 values. Same-recording Fourier torque RMS 0.7709 (left) and 0.9698 (right) N m over 6,986 joint-time rows (Table 3); identified armature groups about 1.5, 0.57, 0.29 kg m$^2$ for J1-J2, J3-J4, J5-J7 (Table 4). Held out (sec. IV-A4, App. C.3): one 32.6503 s teleoperation recording 'excluded from mechanical identification and servo-gain search'; external position targets pass through simulated motion-controller shaping (PVT interpolation, 5 Hz second-order Butterworth, 11 ms command period) into a PD servo $\tau_{\mathrm{PD},j} = K_{p,j}(q_j^c - q_j) + K_{d,j}(\dot{q}_j^c - \dot{q}_j)$ ($q_j^c$ the commanded, $q_j$ the simulated position; gains per joint in Table C3) driving the identified MuJoCo model at 1 kHz (1 ms steps); per joint, over the $M = 3{,}165$ aligned measured-time samples after a 1 s warm-up, $\mathrm{RMSE}_q = \sqrt{\frac{1}{M}\sum_{k=1}^{M} (q^{\mathrm{sim}}_{j,k} - q^{\mathrm{meas}}_{j,k})^2}$ in rad and $\mathrm{RMSE}_\tau = \sqrt{\frac{1}{M}\sum_{k=1}^{M} (\tau^{\mathrm{PD}}_{j,k} - \tau_{I,j,k})^2}$ in N m, both uncentred: position 0.00614 (right J2) to 0.03522 (left J7) rad, torque 0.73545 (left J3) to 4.00099 (right J1) N m (Table C3). Object and cross-engine protocol (sec. IV-B, App. D): five assets (kettle, gum box, sponge, shuttlecock, pen), one real recorded interaction each; the G2-Swiftpicker robot configuration is fixed (Table D1) and recorded joint and gripper position commands drive the robot at about 100 Hz zero-order hold with 1 ms physics; objects are free rigid bodies. Bounded effective object parameters are fitted in MuJoCo 3.10.0 CPU (soft contact, solref/solimp), the candidate is frozen as an MJB and replayed in Newton 1.4.0 / MuJoCo-Warp 3.10.0 CUDA (SolverMuJoCo, same contact family) and in PhysX (Isaac Sim 6.0.0 RC, CPU TGS, 32/1 solver iterations, 1 ms step; App. D.6) built 'from frozen numeric arrays' (Table 2). Observation error $\mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\mathrm{mean}_t \|\mathbf{p}^{\mathrm{sim}}_t - \mathbf{p}^{\mathrm{obs}}_t\|^2}$ over valid observation timestamps $t$, in mm for RGB-D 3D points or px for image points (sec. III-C); fitting objectives $J_{3D} = (e_{3D}/0.01\,\mathrm{m})^2 + 0.1\,(e_{\mathrm{hold}}/0.03\,\mathrm{rad})^2$ (eq. 6; $e_{3D}$ training-window centre RMSE, $e_{\mathrm{hold}}$ holding-gripper RMSE) and $J_{\mathrm{RGB}} = e_{\mathrm{RGB}} + 150\, e_{\mathrm{dual}}$ (App. D; $e_{\mathrm{RGB}}$ in px, $e_{\mathrm{dual}}$ dual-gripper RMSE in rad). Results: kettle lid-centre RMSE 39.56 to 25.24 mm (MuJoCo), 40.98 to 25.12 (MJWarp), 38.66 to 26.23 (PhysX); gum box 12.78 to 12.23, 13.37 to 13.58, 10.99 to 11.46 mm; sponge frozen transfer to PhysX 25.50 to 524.61 mm with failure to lift (App. D.3); native PhysX recovery with common finger contact 800 N/m stiffness and 5 N s/m damping (sponge) and common angular damping 20 s$^{-1}$ (shuttlecock) and 500 s$^{-1}$ (pen) applied to both baseline and fitted models restores completion (sponge 2/2 to 4/4, handovers 2/2 to 2/2 replays of one real episode); under matched native settings sponge friction refit 3.0 to 1.2 moves full centre RMSE 41.54 to 26.73 mm while vertical error grows 13.40 to 19.38 mm and maximum effective hand penetration stays 35.82 to 32.79 mm (App. D.5); shuttlecock 20.47 to 21.05 px (worse), pen 9.72 to 9.31 px (0.408 px, below about 3 px annotation uncertainty) (sec. IV-B2). 'Repeat ranges are all-repeat min-max, not confidence intervals' (App. D.4).
load_bearing_assumption: That a Pearson correlation across 22 heterogeneous (robot, task, policy) triples whose real Scores spread from 0.24 to 1.00 measures how faithfully the simulator reproduces the real robot, rather than how much task difficulty varies between tasks. The paper itself hedges the number to 'descriptive' and states 'These describe task-specific Score differences, not success-rate differences or uncertainty intervals' (sec. II-E). Arithmetic on Table B1 (operator computation): the between-pair standard deviation of real Scores is 0.207 and the gap RMSE is 0.052, so $r \approx \sqrt{1 - 0.052^2/0.195^2} = 0.964$ follows from the gap-to-spread ratio; a simulator that reproduced each task's difficulty only to within $\pm 0.1$ would score $r > 0.95$ on this spread. The second assumption is that 'equal counts' of 30-100 rollouts resolve the per-pair gap: under the binomial bound on the standard error of a bounded per-episode mean (SE 0.03-0.085 per pair), only 1 of 22 gaps (G2 Swiftpicker Select by Color, $\Delta = -0.10$, $n = 100$) exceeds 1.96 standard errors of the difference, so the table cannot tell a perfect simulator from one wrong by $\pm 0.08$ on any single task; the CL-W43-02 red team showed a perfect simulator produces exactly this agreement pattern. Third, that manual real scoring and automatic simulated scoring apply one criterion ('Test personnel ... assign the scores manually and adjudicate failures and timeouts. Simulation scores are assigned automatically', sec. II-C). Fourth, that the identified-robot replay and the object studies, which the paper says 'do not establish an asset-linked benchmark benefit' (sec. IV-A) and 'do not establish a causal reduction in benchmark task-score discrepancy' (sec. IV-B3), nonetheless support the claim that the benchmark's fidelity is 'evidence-led'.
weakest_component: The 22-pair headline table. (1) Eight of the 22 pairs are imported from Genie Sim 3.0 with no system identification ('we did not perform system identification specifically for G1', sec. II-C) and no stated policy; the remaining 14 are the same pairs that appear as the 'before/after' comparison, so the paper has 14 new (robot, task) pairs, not 22 plus 14. (2) Every point is a different policy on a different task, so $r$ never compares two policies on one task; the correlation reports whether a real-fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ finds the simulated copy about as hard as the real cell, which is the easiest direction (sim-trained policies, where the lane's exploit question lives, are never evaluated). (3) No per-pair interval, no repeated real batch, no chance-agreement baseline; the paper's own captions say so three times (Table B1, App. C.3, App. D.5). (4) The scoring channel differs by world: manual adjudication of failures and timeouts in real, automatic in sim (sec. II-C); the stage credits that make up Score are not published ('The source provides neither evaluation counts nor exact phase definitions', Fig. E1). (5) The physics layer is single-episode throughout: 'Each asset has one recorded real interaction' (sec. IV-B1); the 'held-out' windows 'are later segments of the same recording; whole-trajectory feasibility gates and development inspection mean they are not blind independent tests' (sec. III-C); the cross-engine recovery is by hand-set damping ('Strong damping is an effective engine adaptation rather than measured rolling friction', App. D.2) with 'no real contact-force reference' (sec. III-C); the 'Implementation details pending' and 'Configuration records pending' paragraphs (App. C.3, Table D1) say the executable configurations behind the robot replay are not archived. (6) Which engine and which solver settings ran the 22 task-level simulated evaluations is unknown (not in text): the object study names MuJoCo, MJWarp and PhysX, the task study names only 'a fixed Genie Sim experimental branch' (sec. II-C).
regime: Robots: G1 Omnipicker (8 pairs), G2 Swiftpicker (6), G2 Wuji (1), Arx X5 (7) for the task study; G2 crsB dual 7-joint arms for identification (both grippers removed, fixed base); Arx X5 'lacks force control' and gets a simplified model (sec. IV-A). Engines: task-level simulation on 'a fixed Genie Sim experimental branch' (engine and solver settings not stated); object study on MuJoCo 3.10.0 CPU, MuJoCo-Warp 3.10.0 CUDA via Newton 1.4.0 SolverMuJoCo, PhysX in Isaac Sim 6.0.0 RC with CPU TGS, 32/1 solver iterations, 1 ms step (Table 2, App. D.6); robot replay in MuJoCo at 1 kHz with an 11 ms command period (App. C.3). Policy class: $\pi_{0.5}$ with SFT on real-robot data per task, inference in both worlds (G2, Arx); G1 policy unknown (not in text). Tasks (Table A1, 16 names): Grasp Target Object, Select by Color, Recognize Size, Apply Common Sense, Follow Logic (OR) (selection and reasoning); Place Object Into Box Color, Pack In Supermarket, Sort Fruit, Place Block Into Drawer, Place Bottle On Coaster (placement and sorting); Bimanual Chip Handover; Stack Blocks; Fold Towel, Fold The Clothes In Half, Folding Clothes, Fold Cloth (textile). Episodes: 30, 50 or 100 per pair and world, 1,340 per world in total (operator sum of Table B1). Real Score band 0.24-1.00; $\Delta_i \in [-0.110, +0.080]$. Identification data: 18 recordings per arm (7 friction, 10 sine, 1 coupled Fourier of about 100 s), 3,696 scored time rows per arm (App. C.1); held-out teleoperation 32.6503 s, 3,165 scored samples. Object data: kettle 260 RGB-D lid observations, gum box 127, sponge 92 over 9.21 s, shuttlecock 12 RGB points with 3 valid depths, pen 11 RGB points (Table 5); 15 case-stack comparisons. Compute, wall-clock and dollar cost: unknown (not in text). Date: arXiv 2026-11-11, v1; venue not stated.
information_asymmetry: (1) Per-episode vs aggregate. The real side holds 1,340 scored episodes with stage credits $c_{is}$, adjudicated failure stages and timeouts, and 100 Hz joint traces and motor currents; the validation reads 22 numbers from it and one correlation from those. What would grade the simulator per pair exists and is discarded: the per-pair standard error (binomial bound 0.03-0.085; only 1 of 22 gaps exceeds 1.96 standard errors of the difference, operator computation), the stage at which real and simulated episodes fail ('completed substeps and failure stages', sec. II-A; Fig. E1 gives stage rates without 'evaluation counts'), and whether a simulated episode reaching the same Score takes the same path. (2) What the simulator knows about itself and never reports upward. The object study names the numerics (1 ms step, PhysX TGS with 32/1 iterations, MuJoCo solref/solimp soft contact, 'GPU repeat variation' in MJWarp, 35.82 mm effective hand penetration) and shows one engine swap at identical parameters moving error from 25.50 to 524.61 mm (App. D.3); the 22 task Scores are computed on an unnamed engine and setting, and no $\Delta_i$ is ever read against a solver-iteration or time-step change. (3) Same policy, different worlds, 22 different policies. Each pair runs one real-data-fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ in both worlds; robot, task and policy vary together across the 22 points, so the correlation measures difficulty reproduction for policies that never saw the simulator's pixels and have no incentive to exploit it. A sim-trained arm on the same tasks is missing; the lane's exploit question is unanswerable from this design. (4) Ideas: per-pair interval and failure-stage disagreement as the reported columns; re-scoring the 22 simulated evaluations under a solver-iteration and time-step sweep to see which $\Delta_i$ move (the per-step audit applied to a validated benchmark); the chance-agreement $r$ implied by the spread-to-RMSE ratio; a sim-trained arm on the same pairs.
occupies: Published: the Genie Sim Benchmark real-sim Score table for 22 (robot, task) pairs on G1 Omnipicker, G2 Swiftpicker, G2 Wuji and Arx X5 with real-data-SFT $\pi_{0.5}$ policies and equal rollout counts (Pearson $r = 0.9686$, MAE 0.0405, RMSE 0.0520, $\Delta_i \in [-0.110, +0.080]$, Table B1); the 14-pair before/after system-identification comparison ($r$ 0.9518 to 0.9669, MAE down 20.0%, RMSE down 15.6%, Table B2); a three-stage constrained current-to-torque identification of both G2 crsB arms (98 unknowns per arm, Huber losses, PSD pseudo-inertia, Tables 3-4) with a 32.65 s teleoperation replay through a motion-controller plus PD chain (position RMSE 0.00614-0.03522 rad, torque 0.73545-4.00099 N m, Table C3); and five single-episode object fits in MuJoCo frozen and replayed in MuJoCo-Warp and PhysX, including the sponge soft-contact transfer failure (25.50 to 524.61 mm) and its recovery by shared native PhysX stiffness, damping and angular damping (Tables D3, D8-D9). Not claimed and left open: any per-pair uncertainty, chance-corrected agreement or repeated real batch; sensitivity of the 22 Scores to engine, time step or solver iterations; a sim-trained policy on the paired tasks; a real contact-force reference; independent-episode object validation; the engine behind the task-level simulation. Against CL-W43-02 (refuted 2026-10-20): this is not a policy-pair ranking table, so the 'resolvable pairs' ruler does not apply as worded; the sibling fact does, and is conceded in the paper's own captions: the real sample resolves 1 of 22 gaps, which is also what a perfect simulator would produce, so the table cannot distinguish a faithful simulator from one wrong by $\pm 0.08$ per task.

neighbors.title: Evaluating Real-World Robot Manipulation Policies in Simulation (SIMPLER)
neighbors.trick: Match the simulator's controller and camera image to a real robot cell and show that several generalist policies' success rates in the simulated cell line up with their real ones; this paper cites it as [1] for the paired-evaluation idea and departs by using one task-specific real-fine-tuned policy per pair and a Pearson $r$ over tasks instead of a rank metric over policies.

neighbors.title: Validating Robotics Simulators on Real-World Impacts
neighbors.trick: Toss a cube and land a biped on a real rig, fit each simulator's contact parameters to the recordings, and show Drake, MuJoCo and Bullet get inelastic impacts right and elastic impacts wrong; cited as [2] for validation against real trajectories, and the register this paper's object replays imitate with one episode per asset and no contact-force reference.

neighbors.title: Sim2Real Predictivity: Does Evaluation in Simulation Predict Real-World Performance?
neighbors.trick: Run nine navigation agents in a scanned replica and on the robot, define the sim-vs-real correlation coefficient, find it low (0.18) because agents exploit wall-sliding in simulation, and tune the simulator until it rises (0.844); cited as [4]; the origin of the correlation-as-validity metric, and the one neighbour that measured exploitation by sim-trained agents, which this paper's real-trained policies cannot show.

neighbors.title: Genie Sim 3.0: A High-Fidelity Comprehensive Simulation Platform for Humanoid Robot
neighbors.trick: An LLM generates scenes and a VLM scores episodes to mass-produce evaluation scenarios, with a 10,000-hour synthetic dataset shown to transfer zero-shot to the real robot under controlled conditions; the source of this paper's 8 G1 Omnipicker pairs, which carry no system identification and an unstated policy (sec. II-C).

neighbors.title: RoboSimStudio: An Interactive Toolkit for Human and Agent Rapid Real2Sim of Robot Manipulation Tasks
neighbors.trick: Expose solver, contact model and physical parameters as editable choices in Newton so a human or a coding agent can iterate a simulation against observed behaviour, with visual, force-feedback and agentic real2sim2real checks; cited as [8]; the tool-shaped neighbour for the contact-mapping problem this paper hits when a MuJoCo solref/solimp fit has no PhysX equivalent (App. D.3).

theme_fit.why: validation against real data (22 paired task Scores, a held-out joint-trace replay) and model-form disagreement across contact models (the same frozen object parameters give 25.50 mm in MuJoCo and 524.61 mm in PhysX) are two of the lane's three V&V legs, with the numerics named (1 ms, TGS 32/1, solref/solimp, GPU repeat variation) but never tied to the task Scores; the gap it leaves, per-pair uncertainty plus engine-setting sensitivity of a validated benchmark, is a lane-shaped probe under one GPU-week

a simulator-fidelity validity claim whose measurement fails in the lane's sense: one descriptive correlation over 22 heterogeneous pairs, no intervals, manual vs automatic scoring channels, 8 of 22 points imported from a prior paper; supplies the incumbent form of a real-to-sim validity table

limitations_as_complaints: My headline is one correlation with no error bars, and I say so myself: 'These describe task-specific Score differences, not success-rate differences or uncertainty intervals' (sec. II-E); 'Mini-plots show the final gap on a common -0.12 to +0.12 scale, not uncertainty intervals' (Table B1); 'There are no independent repeated real trials or uncertainty intervals in the supplied results' (App. C.3); 'repetition counts therefore do not support confidence intervals or population success rates' (App. D.5) [paraphrase: with 30-100 rollouts per pair, only 1 of 22 gaps is larger than its own sampling noise, operator computation].

My physics layer never validates on anything it did not fit on, and it does not reach the task Scores: 'The \"held-out\" time windows are later segments of the same recording; whole-trajectory feasibility gates and development inspection mean they are not blind independent tests' (sec. III-C); 'Each asset has one recorded real interaction' (sec. IV-B1); 'These robot-level evaluations do not establish an asset-linked benchmark benefit' (sec. IV-A); 'The current results do not establish a causal reduction in benchmark task-score discrepancy' (sec. IV-B3); 'Successful execution alone therefore cannot establish an identification benefit' (sec. IV-B3).

My cross-engine contact transfer is rescued by hand-set damping and stiffness with no force measurement to check against: 'Native simulated contact forces use different readback semantics, and no real contact-force reference is supplied' (sec. III-C); 'Strong damping is an effective engine adaptation rather than measured rolling friction' (App. D.2); 'The source path does not express MuJoCo solref/solimp equivalently ... Geometry, initialization, robot/observation calibration and numerical differences remain potential contributors' (App. D.3); 'It does not rule out other model and solver differences' (App. D.2); and the executable configurations are not archived: 'Exact limiter thresholds, coupling rules and filter recurrences/initial states ... still require executable configuration records' (App. C.3).
